title: Rhetoric and persuasion
summary: The persuasive toolkit of speeches, adverts and opinion writing: appeals to ethos, pathos and logos, and patterned devices such as anaphora, tricolon and antithesis.

keyterms.definition: Persuasion through the speaker's credibility, character or authority.
Persuasion through appeals to the audience's emotions.
Persuasion through logic, evidence, statistics and reasoning.
Repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses or sentences.
A group of three parallel words, phrases or clauses, also called the rule of three.
Placing contrasting ideas in parallel structures, e.g. 'not a burden but a gift'.
A question asked for effect rather than to get an answer, guiding the audience to a conclusion.
Words like 'we', 'us' and 'our' that bind speaker and audience together.
A command form of the verb, e.g. 'Act now', urging the audience to act.
A short personal story used to illustrate a point and build connection.
Choosing the right moment or occasion for a persuasive message, linking it to timely events.
Repeating a grammatical structure across phrases or sentences for rhythm and emphasis.

questions.prompt: "As a nurse who has worked night shifts for twenty years, I can tell you this policy will fail." Which appeal dominates?
questions.explanation: The speaker establishes credibility through professional experience, which is ethos.

questions.prompt: "Four out of five households now spend more on energy than on food." Which appeal is this?
questions.explanation: Statistics appeal to reason (logos), though numbers can also be chosen to provoke emotion.

questions.text: An appeal to the audience's emotions is called ___.
questions.explanation: Pathos uses emotive language, images and anecdotes to make audiences feel.

questions.statement: A single sentence can combine ethos, pathos and logos.
questions.explanation: Skilled persuaders blend appeals; analysis should explain how they reinforce each other.

questions.prompt: A charity appeal opens: "Last winter, eight-year-old Sami did his homework by candlelight, wrapped in his coat." Which techniques are used?
questions.explanation: A named child's story personalises the issue and triggers sympathy.

questions.prompt: Match the appeal to the example.

pairs.right: It costs less than a coffee a day
Don't let her face this alone
With the election only days away…

questions.explanation: Kairos ties the message to a timely moment, adding urgency.

questions.text: Linking a persuasive message to the right moment or occasion is called ___.
questions.explanation: Speeches often gain power from timing: anniversaries, crises or elections.

questions.prompt: "We will not stand by while our children inherit a poisoned planet." What does 'we' and 'our' achieve?
options: They distance the speaker from the audience
They create unity and shared responsibility
They make the sentence a question
questions.explanation: Inclusive pronouns build a collective identity between speaker and audience.

questions.statement: Logos is always more honest than pathos.
questions.explanation: Statistics can be selective or misleading; any appeal can be used manipulatively or ethically.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a classic persuasive speech structure.
questions.explanation: Many speeches follow this arc, building from attention to action.

questions.prompt: "We will rebuild. We will recover. We will rise." Identify the main device.
questions.explanation: Repeating 'We will' at the start of each sentence creates momentum and determination (it is also a tricolon).

questions.text: A group of three parallel phrases, such as "faster, cleaner, cheaper", is a ___.
questions.explanation: Three items feel complete and memorable, so the pattern is common in slogans and speeches.

questions.prompt: "This is not the end of our story; it is the beginning." What device structures this sentence?
questions.explanation: Contrasting 'end' and 'beginning' in parallel clauses sharpens the reframing.

questions.statement: "Can we really afford to wait any longer?" is a rhetorical question that steers the audience towards answering 'no'.
questions.explanation: Rhetorical questions position the audience to agree without the speaker stating the claim directly.

questions.prompt: Match the device to the example.

pairs.right: Who among us has not felt afraid?
Every child, every school, every day

questions.explanation: Identifying the device is a start; explain how it moves the audience.

questions.text: A command such as "Join us now" uses the ___ mood.
questions.explanation: Imperatives create urgency and direct the audience to act.

questions.prompt: Why are patterned devices such as anaphora and tricolon especially common in speeches?
options: Listeners cannot reread, so rhythm and repetition aid memory and impact
questions.explanation: Spoken texts depend on the ear; repetition structures ideas and invites applause.

questions.statement: Parallelism means using contradictory words together.
questions.explanation: Parallelism repeats a grammatical structure; contradictory words together form an oxymoron.

questions.prompt: "They called us dreamers. They called us naïve. They called us too young to matter." What is the cumulative effect?
options: It builds a sense of defiance against repeated dismissal
It shows the speaker agrees with critics
It creates a calm, neutral tone
questions.explanation: Anaphora with escalating insults sets up a turn in which the speaker can refute them.

questions.prompt: Which is the best analytical sentence about a tricolon?
options: The tricolon "safer, fairer, greener" builds a rhythmic, complete vision, making the policy sound comprehensive and hard to oppose.
questions.explanation: It quotes the device, names it and explains its effect in relation to purpose.
